edges.relationship: Davidoff credits Douglas’s account of pollution and boundaries with changing her interpretation of domestic service, household routines and respectable status.
edges.evidence_note: Davidoff’s own 1995 account recalls discovering Purity and Danger in the early 1970s. She connects its concepts to evangelical cleanliness, household space and the incorporation of new wealth, while explaining that subsequent feminist analysis went beyond Douglas. The 1966 book itself was not newly read; 1995 is the acknowledgment, not the date of first influence.

edges.relationship: As Catherine Hall explains, Davidoff developed Weber’s questions about modernity, power, market position and status through a feminist account of gender and family.
edges.evidence_note: Hall’s 2015 tribute says Weber probably did more than any other social theorist to frame Davidoff’s thinking. The qualified attribution and Davidoff’s feminist transformation are retained. This is Hall’s substantive interpretation, not a claim that Davidoff accepted an entire Weberian system; the complete tribute and Davidoff’s underlying books remain unread here.

edges.relationship: A comparison of their contributions to Family Fortunes highlights Davidoff’s sociological approach and Hall’s Marxist-feminist interests in their joint account of family, gender and class.
edges.evidence_note: An editorial teaching comparison grounded in Cornelie Usborne’s 2015 account of their complementary approaches, not a direction of influence inferred from coauthorship. Usborne also describes the 1973 project proposal; Hall’s own tribute confirms their coauthorship and describes Davidoff’s methods. Equal authorship is retained. The complete 1987 book and later introductions were not freshly read; the later reissue is not a new original contribution.

edges.relationship: McClintock credits Davidoff’s pioneering work but criticizes her Cullwick interpretation for reproducing Munby’s image of control and obscuring the servant’s constrained agency.
edges.evidence_note: The 1995 argument was read in Plinio Dentzien’s authorized Portuguese translation (2003), printed pp. 13 and 17–20. McClintock acknowledges her debt to Davidoff and to Davidoff and Hall’s joint Family Fortunes, then makes the particular agency criticism of Davidoff’s Munby–Cullwick essay. She also rejects a picture of equal power: agency within severe social inequality is the point. The English chapter and Davidoff’s original essay were not freshly read; this is not a blanket rejection of their work.

edges.relationship: McClintock explicitly draws on Davidoff’s domestic-service research and Davidoff and Hall’s joint Family Fortunes in her account of gender, class and domestic power (1995).
edges.evidence_note: McClintock’s substantive discussion and explicit acknowledgment in note 3 identify these resources; her later criticism of Davidoff’s particular Cullwick interpretation coexists with this debt. Hall retains equal credit for the joint book. Selected passages were freshly read in Plinio Dentzien’s authorized 2003 Portuguese translation of the 1995 chapter; the English original and the cited Davidoff texts were not freshly read. This does not imply wholesale agreement or personal mentoring.

edges.relationship: Dickason praises Carter’s corrective history of western Canada but argues that it idealizes Indigenous societies and generalizes equality too broadly (2001).
edges.evidence_note: A bounded criticism within an appreciative review of Aboriginal People and Colonizers of Western Canada to 1900. The substantive review is reproduced in the institutional repository’s abstract field; that primary text was read, but the PDF returned 403 and was not facsimile-collated. Carter’s book body remains unread. Dickason’s separate buffalo example is not needed to substantiate this relationship.

edges.relationship: Dickason questions Pagden’s account of rejected imperial doctrines by distinguishing theoretical argument from their continued use in practical colonial policy (1997).
edges.evidence_note: Review of Lords of All the World, especially its treatment of Hostiensis and Edward Coke. She also praises the book’s contribution to comparative colonial studies; this is not rejection of the whole project. The review’s original heading prints Worlds, whereas the identified 1995 book title uses World. Full review read; Pagden’s book body remains unread.

edges.relationship: Deloria incorporates Dickason’s The Myth of the Savage into his account of critical scholarship on the images and discourses that accompanied conquest, crediting its extension to French contexts (2002).
edges.evidence_note: A named historiographical resource, not personal mentoring or a comprehensive intellectual lineage. Deloria credits Gordon Sayre alongside Dickason. The particular paragraph on p.10 was freshly read and visually checked; Dickason’s book body remains unread. This claim is distinct from Deloria’s already mapped Turner criticism and Wilson resource.

edges.relationship: Medicine’s 2003 review identifies Dickason’s historical insights among the Indigenous scholarly resources Carter uses in her history of Aboriginal people and colonizers in western Canada.
edges.evidence_note: Explicitly attributed to Beatrice Medicine’s substantive review of Carter’s 1999 book, whose body remains unread. Harold Cardinal, Paul Chartrand and Edward Ahenakew retain co-credit. This establishes reported use of historical insight, not mentorship, exclusive influence, or a particular Dickason work. It is distinct from Dickason’s own 2001 criticism of Carter; Medicine’s Big Bear example and Christine Welsh’s formulation are not assigned to Dickason.

edges.relationship: Walker uses Foucault’s hierarchy of knowledge to explain the exclusion and subordination of Māori knowledge in the Native Schools curriculum.
edges.evidence_note: Walker’s own 2016 chapter, p. 24, explicitly cites Foucault (1980) for this interpretation. This is one identified conceptual use in a history of colonial schooling; it does not assign the origin of Māori knowledge, the whole chapter, or Walker’s 1990 book to Foucault. The reference on p. 37 prints the title as Knowledge/Power; Foucault’s original volume was not freshly read.

edges.relationship: Adds and colleagues identify Walker’s use of Gramsci’s paired domination and intellectual-moral leadership to analyse monocultural media and Māori subordination.
edges.evidence_note: Explicitly mediated by the joint 2005 Broadcasting Standards Authority report, not a claim to have read Walker’s 2002 chapter Māori news is bad news. Peter Adds, Maia Bennett, Meegan Hall, Bernard Kernot, Marie Russell and Tai Walker retain joint credit. Their literature review specifically reports the Gramsci citation and its media argument. Tai Walker is a separate coauthor, not Ranginui Walker. No exact Gramsci passage or edition is inferred.

edges.relationship: Byrnes and Coleborne identify Fanon as an intellectual resource for Walker’s counter-history of colonization and analysis of colonial power and resistance.
edges.evidence_note: This is the explicitly named reading of Giselle Byrnes and Catharine Coleborne in their joint 2011 editorial: p. 8 discusses colonial disavowal, and note 48 names the revised 2004 Ka Whawhai Tonu Mātou and Fanon’s The Wretched of the Earth and Black Skin, White Masks. Walker’s book and these Fanon editions were not freshly read. The 2004 witness is not silently backdated to the 1990 original or treated as the sole origin of Māori historiography.

edges.relationship: Linda Tuhiwai Smith uses Walker’s public defense of Māori communities as an example of scholars’ responsibilities toward their people.
edges.evidence_note: In her own 27 March 2022 conversation, answering advice for young Indigenous people entering activism and academic spaces, Smith moves from scholarly usefulness and community love to Walker’s conduct on radio and in interviews. This is an explicit exemplary resource in her argument about scholarly responsibility, not inferred mentoring, co-membership, or the origin of Decolonizing Methodologies. The organizer’s transcript pp. 8–9 was read; the audiovisual performance was not watched.

edges.relationship: Bailyn’s account of culture supplies a starting problem for Iriye’s exploration of connections between local mental worlds and international cultural orders.
edges.evidence_note: The address also credits Franklin and McNeill. No mentoring claim; Bailyn’s original remains unread. Delivered 1988; published 1989.

edges.relationship: Iriye invokes Curtin’s warning against self-knowledge alone when arguing that historians should communicate across cultural boundaries.
edges.evidence_note: Specific methodological use, not career lineage. Curtin’s original address remains unread. Delivered 1988; published 1989.

edges.relationship: Ricœur’s discussion of cultural incommunicability becomes a qualified point of engagement in Iriye’s argument for historical encounter and translation.
edges.evidence_note: Not a refutation of Ricœur. Translator Kelbley and Ninkovich’s recommendation retain credit; original unread. Delivered 1988; published 1989.

edges.relationship: Iriye uses Weber’s nationalism as a contrasting example to show how cultural conceptions organize accounts of international relations.
edges.evidence_note: He grants its relative realism but treats it as situated ideology; no formative influence inferred. Delivered 1988; published 1989.

edges.relationship: Iriye uses Hobsbawm’s treatment of transnational firms in Age of Extremes as an example when explaining historians’ growing attention to non-state actors.
edges.evidence_note: A specific historiographic resource, not personal mentoring. The same passage rejects a direct genealogy from Marxism to recent transnational historiography. Selected tool-extracted primary text, not facsimile-collated; Hobsbawm’s cited book remains unread.

edges.relationship: Corbin credits reading Febvre during his university training with orienting him toward historical psychology and the history of sensibilities.
edges.evidence_note: Corbin’s own 1993 interview says Michel de Bouard recommended Febvre and that Corbin repeatedly returned to his work. De Bouard retains this mediating teaching role. This is a named formative reading, not an inference from Annales affiliation, exclusive sensory-history priority or direct personal instruction by Febvre. Only the interview’s printed p. 7 was freshly checked; Febvre’s complete books and the remaining interview pages were not read here.

edges.relationship: Corbin explains his departure from Labrousse’s economic-to-mentalities model when subsistence practices and unreliable statistics frustrated his study of the Limousin.
edges.evidence_note: Own interview given in 2003, read in Christian Pierre Kasper’s 2005 Portuguese translation, pp. 14–15. Corbin describes abandoning much of the model, not every quantitative method or all of Labrousse’s work. Bertrand Gille, whom Labrousse recommended, was his actual supervisor and helped prompt the methodological change; Labrousse is not silently substituted for Gille.

edges.relationship: Corbin reports Prost’s criticism that his historical practice gives insufficient attention to history’s civic and social mission.
edges.evidence_note: Explicitly Corbin’s own recollection in the 2006 Vacarme interview, not a newly located text by Prost. Corbin acknowledges that the description may be right and explains his resistance to lessons-of-history arguments. His later 2013 interview also recalls Prost’s contrast between civic mission and writing for pleasure. This is a specific disagreement between colleagues, not generalized hostility or rejection of the quality of Corbin’s research.

edges.relationship: Corbin uses Foucault’s analysis of medical attention to sexuality and sexual classification to frame his own questions about bodily practices before the later nineteenth century.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2003 interview read in the credited 2005 translation, pp. 29–30. He praises La Volonté de savoir and explicitly invokes Foucault’s argument, while distinguishing his interest in the period before the post-1860 taxonomy of perversions. This is specified use and development, not wholesale Foucauldian affiliation or a claim that Foucault’s text directly records sexual acts. Foucault’s original book was not freshly read.

edges.relationship: Corbin explicitly rejects the irreversible civilizing trajectory he associates with Elias, emphasizing divergent temporalities and the contingency of historical change.
edges.evidence_note: Corbin’s own characterization in a 2006 answer about rethinking nineteenth-century political history. The relationship records his particular objection; it does not adopt his description as a complete account of Elias’s argument. Elias’s original works were not freshly checked, and no reply by Elias is asserted.

edges.relationship: Corbin criticizes the republic-centered account he associates with Furet for reducing much of nineteenth-century France to steps toward a later republican outcome.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2006 answer also names Maurice Agulhon, whose credit is retained here without inventing a standalone endpoint. Corbin argues for studying monarchies, conflicting political emotions and other periods on their own terms. This records his specific historiographical criticism, not a claim that all of Furet’s work is teleological; Furet’s original books remain unread in this dossier.

edges.relationship: Corbin identifies a limit of the material anthropology associated with Braudel: reconstructing objects and environments does not by itself recover an individual’s inner life.
edges.evidence_note: A narrow methodological objection in Corbin’s 2006 answer about accessing people who left few traces. He acknowledges how much tools and material objects can reveal. The criticism does not deny the value of material history, assert that Braudel attempted a particular biography, or imply that Corbin recovered Pinagot’s own feelings. No complete Braudel work was freshly read.

edges.relationship: Corbin invokes a discussion with Le Goff about the limits of knowing historical individuals when explaining why reconstructing Pinagot’s world cannot recover his private feelings.
edges.evidence_note: Corbin recalls Le Goff’s observation that very few medieval lives allow close personal knowledge, and uses it to distinguish a surrounding historical world from intimacy. Interview given in 2003, read in Kasper’s 2005 translation, p. 24. This is Corbin’s reported use of a methodological discussion, not Le Goff’s endorsement of Pinagot, formal supervision or a claim to read Le Goff’s original biographies. The meeting is not assigned an invented date.
